title: Capacitance and capacitor energy; Electric field strength and field lines; Capacitor charging and discharging
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EL10-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; EL10-1#t4 term and clue written for the game; EL10-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; F03-1#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EL09-3#N.4, EL10-1#N.4b, F03-1#N.2, EL10-1#N.8, F03-1#N.11.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Current
items.clue: Equal to the gradient of a Q–t graph.

items.label: Charge
items.clue: Equal to the area under an I–t graph.

items.label: Exponential decay
items.clue: Fall in which the rate of loss is proportional to the amount left.

items.label: Field lines
items.clue: Drawn starting on + and ending on –, closer together where E is stronger; they never cross.

questions.stem: Four identical capacitors, each of capacitance C, are first connected all in parallel, giving an equivalent capacitance C_X. They are then reconnected all in series, giving an equivalent capacitance C_Y. How does C_X compare with C_Y?

options.text: C_X is the same as C_Y.

questions.stem: A capacitor is charged through a resistor by a battery. At time t₁ the p.d. across the capacitor is one quarter of the battery's emf. At a later time t₂ it is three quarters of the emf. What is the current at t₂ divided by the current at t₁?
questions.explanation: Current = (p.d. across the resistor) ÷ R. At t₁ that p.d. is ¾ of the emf; at t₂ it is ¼. Ratio: ¼ ÷ ¾ = 1/3.

questions.stem: At point P, a charge of +2.0 µC experiences an electric force of 5.0 × 10⁻³ N directed east. This charge is removed and a charge of −6.0 µC is placed at P; the charges that produce the field do not move. Taking east as positive, what is the electric force on the −6.0 µC charge?

An uncharged capacitor is charged through a 3.0 kΩ resistor by an ideal battery of emf 9.0 V, all connected in series. What is the current in the resistor at the instant when the potential difference across the capacitor is 6.0 V?

The field lines of a long, straight charged wire spread out radially, in planes at right angles to the wire: they spread in two dimensions, not three. Point P is 2.0 cm from the wire and point Q is 6.0 cm from it, both far from the wire's ends. How does the electric field strength at P compare with that at Q?

options.text: E at P is 9 times E at Q, as the field strength falls with the square of the distance.
E at P is 3 times E at Q, as the same lines spread over 3 times the area at Q.
E is the same at P and Q, as every line that passes P also passes Q.
E at Q is 3 times E at P, as the larger cylinder at Q holds more lines.
